extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of language, and metaphysics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles about names, definitions, connotation/denotation, categories, and syllogistic reasoning in formal logic and philosophy of language. Targets how to form, test, and use definitions and propositions correctly in logical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hedge vague connotative names for accurate reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a term is wholly unfit for accurate reasoning, unless hedged round on every occasion by other phrases; as building stone, precious stone, gall-stone, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the familiar term 'stone' applies to many disparate things and lacks a uniformly present quality, so definitions and reasoning using such words must qualify them (building stone, precious stone) to avoid confusion. Methods of definition are baffled where community of application is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a term for 'to connote' in a precise technical sense
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an urgent necessity for a term exclusively appropriated to express the manner in which a concrete general name serves to mark the attributes which are involved in its signification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although James Mill and others use 'to connote' more widely, the author recommends adopting a precise technical sense (as in scholastic usage) to distinguish this particular kind of involving/ implying and to avoid conflating different senses (e.g., involve, imply). The schoolmen used 'connote' to mean forms/attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test a name's denotation by what it can be predicated of
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of what a name denotes is what it can be predicated of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining denotation is practical: judge what can be truly predicated using the name. Example used in discussion of negative names—if you can predicate 'not-white' of a sound or smell, that bears on the denotation of the negative name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat affirmation and negation as jointly exhaustive for a given attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: The affirmation and the negation of the same attribute cannot but divide the whole field of predication between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter-argument to Bain's narrower view of negative names: negation of an attribute (e.g., 'not-white') is not limited to some subclass (e.g., 'colored things other than white') but, properly understood, covers the complement of the attribute across predication. Use this principle when classifying names and predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: View the Categories as generalizations of predicates (analysis of predication)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Categories do not seem to have been intended as a classification of Namable Things ... They seem to have been rather intended as a generalization of predicates; an analysis of the final import of predication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using Categories (e.g., Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation), ask 'Under what Categories can we predicate regarding X?' rather than 'Into what Category is X placed?' Example: for a state of mind like Hope, we predicate Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation about it.

rubrics_metrics.name: For logical purposes, treat classes as indefinite rather than definite
rubrics_metrics.description: I have assumed them to be indefinite; because, for the purposes of Logic, definite classes, as such, are almost useless; though often serviceable as means of abridged expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bain's distinction of definite (enumerated individuals) vs indefinite classes (e.g., men, poets) is noted; for general inference/definition, prefer the indefinite conception of classes to avoid treating trivial enumerations as central to logical form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not elevate Being/Existence to a fictitious summum genus without analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Bain thinks it 'fictitious and unmeaning language' to carry up the classification of Nature to one summum genus, Being, or that which Exists; ... I accept fully Mr. Bain's Law of Relativity, but I do not understand by it that to enable us to apprehend any fact, it is necessary that we should contrast it with some other positive fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence should be handled carefully: it is different from Causation or Co-existence and can be predicated apart from them. The relative opposite of Being is Nonentity; consciousness can require contrast with nonentity or absence as well as another positive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition (Bain's view) as sum of all properties connoted
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition in its full import, is the sum of all the properties connoted by the name; it exhausts the meaning of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bain's doctrine: include all ultimate, underivable properties known to belong (e.g., diamond composed of carbon becomes connoted). The author records and critiques this position, noting consequences where learned scientific facts would become part of common meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish real propositions from verbal ones by common-usage meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition which affirms that an object has a given attribute, while designating the object by a name which already signifies the attribute, adds no information to that which was already possessed by all who understood the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author objects to absorbing learned/scientific properties into the common meaning of a term: the meaning of a word should be what is connoted in the general mind (common usage); additional specialist facts should not make an assertion 'merely verbal' if those facts are not part of ordinary signification. Use this to decide whether a proposition conveys genuine information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whately's notion of Real Definition (explain more than name implies)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Real Definition is one which 'explains any thing more of the nature of the thing than is implied in the name;' (including under the word 'implied,' not only what the name connotes, but every thing which can be deduced by reasoning from the attributes connoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'real definitions' as descriptions that add explanatory or scientific content beyond ordinary meaning—useful in scientific or technical contexts where special connotation is established; otherwise call such expositions 'descriptions'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate definition with factual premises in syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: In syllogisms (e.g., dragon—serpent—some serpents breathe flame) the definition is not the same as a statement of fact; a premise that is a definition does not establish a factual conclusion unless the factual premise is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating syllogisms, distinguish whether a premise is definitional (true by meaning) or factual (asserting existence). In examples involving imaginary beings, predicates that assert reality must be handled separately; adjust predicates to mark 'imagined' where appropriate ('some serpents are imagined to breathe flame').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard propositional transformations and recognize equivalent forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The different cases of Equipollency, or 'Equivalent Propositional Forms,' are set forth ... One common change of expression, that from affirming a proposition to denying its negative, or vice versa, is designated Obversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be familiar with conversions: contraries, subtraries, contradictories, subalternation, obversion, etc., and apply them correctly when testing logical equivalence or deriving valid forms. Examples and canonical relations between All/No/Some formulations are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about treating attributes as genera/species (courtesy only)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the distinction of Kinds, in the sense explained by us, not being in any way applicable to attributes, it of course follows that although attributes may be put into classes, those classes can be admitted to be genera or species only by courtesy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributes differ from things, so classifications that treat attributes as true genera/species are only approximate. Avoid importing the full genus/species machinery intended for things into the treatment of attributes without qualification.
